note: Floors are per split, in execution accuracy percent, taken as the minimum observed across the recent runs on Mini-Dev (G 9120c2b, H d5927b0, I 700529b, J 4ad0181, 1.0.0 run 39762058351, and the 13-arm runs since), applied to the full split — 498 question ids across 500 rows, of which 496 can be judged by an executable gold statement, and 496 is the denominator every published rate on Mini-Dev uses. A rerun may land below a floor by tolerancePp before the gate fails, because ADR-166 measured that anything inside 4pp cannot be separated from sampling noise at n=239. `inline+retrieval`, `inline+icl`, `inline+repair`, `inline+repair-raw`, `select`, `select5` and `values` were added to the chain after those runs and have no floors yet: the gate records their first measurement and says so rather than inventing a threshold. A run scored on fewer than 95% of the baseline sample fails as a changed sample. `armsBySplit` states which arms each split runs; the dev split compares against a published leaderboard, needs five arms rather than thirteen, and now carries floors of its own taken from the two runs of `40202780469` and `40245630669` — the split that decides adoption is the split that must also guard against regression. A floor is a claim about three coordinates — split, arms, and model — and the model was the one missing: `bird-model.yml` therefore skipped this tool entirely for cross-model runs, which also skipped the funnel, cost and empty-lever checks. `floorModel` states the model each floor was taken on, and a run by another model is measured rather than failed while every structural check still applies. `scoredBySplit` does the same for the sample size: the dev split was being compared against Mini-Dev's 500, so a dev run scoring 600 of 1,532 questions passed a check whose whole job is to notice a shrunken sample. A floor is also a claim about which second model wrote the cross candidates: `select-cross` draws one of its three prompts from a second model, so its dev floor (61.7, run 40806666847) is recorded in `floorSecondModel.dev` and a run that used another second model is measured rather than failed — the same treatment `floorModel` gives the primary model. The arm is listed in `armsBySplit.dev` even though routine dev runs do not request it, because a floor that no arm list mentions is a floor nothing will notice. The `select-cross` floor is the `deepseek-chat` observation (61.7). The same arm measured 61.6 with `glm-4-flash` as the second model (run 40817333043), which is a measurement under a different second model and is therefore not enforced: a floor is one point in a three-coordinate space, and a run that changes a coordinate produces a reading rather than a verdict. `recallFloors` guards the other half of a sampling arm: `candidateRecall - selectionLoss = passed`, so a score is the product of a candidate set and a selector, and a run can trade one for the other without the product moving. The floors are the minimum observed across six Mini-Dev runs of the current arm set (40830721508, 40835406287, 40844442393, 40851090483, 40852749682, 40878610004) and four dev runs of `select-cross` (40835164245, 40842268219, 40843792747, 40865112253), rounded down to one decimal, and enforced with the same 4pp tolerance as accuracy because both are proportions over the same questions. The observed run-to-run spread of the ceiling is 0.8-2.6pp, i.e. inside that tolerance. The Mini-Dev accuracy floors for `select`, `select-duo`, `select-mixed` and `select5` were added in the same pass, from the same six runs: they were being measured every push and guarded by nothing. The ceiling floors also record a real trade rather than forbidding it: `select-mixed` carries a 58.8% ceiling against `select`'s 61.6% and returns 57.8% against 56.0%, which is a purchased selector for a named price, and the ceiling floor is what keeps that price visible in every later run. `select-prune` is the first arm floored from two runs of itself (`57f70f71` and `947134b0`): 54.6 and 59.4 are the lower of the two readings on each column, because the runs landed 1.8pp apart on byte-identical prompts, so the difference between them is the draw and only the lower one is a floor. `select-prune` is the first arm floored on the dev split from a single run (`41085194983`, 60.38%): a floor taken from one measurement is a guard against a regression larger than the split's own noise, not a claim about where the arm sits, and the four-point tolerance is what keeps a draw from failing the build. It is recorded now because an arm the dev split runs is an arm the dev gate must be able to notice. The chain was cut from sixteen arms to eleven in the round that priced its bill: `vote`, `select-prune`, `select-duo`, `select-mixed` and `select5` now run on demand, because each of their gaps on 498 questions sat inside its own MDE (0.00 to 1.41pp against 1.26 to 3.33pp), so a push could not produce a verdict for them — only a bill of 12,765 of the 23,840 prompt tokens a question the sixteen-arm chain cost. Their accuracy and ceiling floors were retired with them rather than left behind as floors nothing would notice, and the measurements they enforced are in docs/benchmarks.md under the chain's bill. `select` stays at four calls a case for a reason that is not a delta: it is the only arm that executes the selector path, and an arm that is wired and never run is how `inline+retrieval` was lost. The sample size of each split is a count of *questions*, not of rows: Mini-Dev's file carries 500 rows for 498 ids because 137 and 138 each appear twice, so `scoredBySplit.minidev` is 496 — the pool a rate is computed over, after the two questions whose gold statements the engine refuses. It read 500 and the runner's default sample size read 500 too, which is why every default run declared `requested: 500` against `available: 498` and this gate failed the build with "the run asked for 500 questions and split minidev has 498" (run 41169457147). The runner no longer copies a size at all: no declared limit means the split's own question count (`resolveLimit`). `corpus` and `served` are the two coordinates that were being assumed rather than read. `corpus.minidev` is the digest of the questions every Mini-Dev floor was taken on (`7f9b2384df7fd655`, 500 rows / 498 ids, read by both runs of 2026-11-08); BIRD re-annotated Mini-Dev on 2026-10-28 and this repository downloads the split from a bucket URL rather than a pinned archive, so a run that reads other questions is not failing a floor, it is failing to be about the same corpus. `served` is the base model the endpoint said it used, which is a different claim from `floorModel`: `floorModel` is what the run asked for and `served` is what answered. On 2026-11-08 both Mini-Dev runs asked for `deepseek-chat` and all 6,448 of their answers came back named `deepseek-flash`, so an alias had been re-pointed under every floor in this file while every published run still recorded the name it asked for. A run whose served base differs from this pin is failed, because a floor is a claim about a model and the name that has to match is the one that answered; a run on a split with no pin is measured and told so. `corpus`, `served` and `baseFingerprint` are the three coordinates that were being assumed rather than read. The third is the weights: `floorModel` is an alias the run asked for and `served` is the name that answered, and neither of them changes when the endpoint keeps the name and changes the build behind it. `eval/bird/fingerprint.ts` asks three fixed questions twice each at temperature zero and records `baseFingerprint` in every artifact; the pin is a digest over those answers plus a digest of the questions themselves (`probeSet`), so an edited probe fails the gate instead of silently re-interpreting the pin. The gate refuses to compare four states it cannot compare — no pin, no reading, an unstable reading and a digest over a different number of answered probes — and only a stable digest over the pinned probe set that differs from the pin is a failure. A matching digest is not proof of the same weights; it is a one-sided test, and the side it covers is the one that has already cost this repository a claim. The first pin was taken in `42523664683`: three probes, two draws each, all six answers identical, `170d0beaa768594b` over `deepseek-flash`, for 138 prompt and 10 completion tokens — the whole generator identity for 148 tokens against the 6,448 answers it describes. That the two draws agreed is the branch this design hoped for and not one it could assume: had they disagreed the pin would have stayed unwritten and the gate would have said why.
